unit.title: Perform manual heating, and thermal cutting

summary: This unit teaches you to use an oxy-fuel torch to heat steel for bending, straightening, preheating and freeing seized parts, and to cut steel with an oxy-fuel cutting torch and a plasma cutter. You will learn to prevent fires and protect yourself, set up, light and shut down the gas outfit, control the heat and judge it by colour, make clean, accurate cuts, recognise cut faults and their causes, and report problems.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 2 qualification (MEM22423). It covers two jobs done with a flame: **manual heating** (heating steel with a torch to bend it, straighten it, preheat it before welding, or free a seized part) and **thermal cutting** (cutting steel with an oxy-fuel cutting torch, and cutting thinner metal with a plasma cutter).

Every fabrication shop, garage, sugar factory, port and construction site in Jamaica uses these skills: cutting plate and sections to size, cutting out old steelwork, freeing rusted bolts on trucks and farm machinery, bending bars for gates and grilles, and straightening parts bent by welding or by accident. The torch is one of the most useful tools in the trade, and one of the most dangerous if it is used carelessly.

**Who it is for:** trainees on the Welding Level 2 programme at HEART/NSTA Trust and other training centres. You will work on mild steel flat bar and plate with an oxy-acetylene outfit, and on thin sheet with a plasma cutter.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the workshop
rows: Plan and prepare
Read the drawing or job sheet, do a risk assessment, choose the nozzle and pressures from the maker's chart, and clean the metal.
Work safely and prevent fire
Wear the right PPE, clear or cover anything that can burn, get a hot work permit where needed, and keep a fire watch.
Set up and shut down the outfit
Check and assemble cylinders, regulators, arrestors, hoses and torch; leak-test, purge, light and set the flame; shut down in the right order.
Heat and bend
Preheat, free seized parts, and heat and bend bar evenly to a marked line, judging the heat by colour or with a temperature crayon.
Straighten by flame
Find a bow, place V-heats on the right side, keep to a dull red, and check between heats.
Cut with oxy-fuel
Start at an edge or pierce a hole, cut on the waste side of the line at a steady speed, and make square, clean cuts.
Cut with plasma
Set up the cutter and air supply safely, and make straight cuts in thin sheet.
Check and report
Judge cut quality, name faults and their causes, clean the work, and report equipment faults and incidents.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on planning, safety, gases and cylinders, equipment, lighting and flames, heating, flame straightening, cutting, cut quality, plasma cutting and shut-down.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact trade words such as kerf, piercing, pilot arc, check valve and contents gauge) and longer answers in full sentences.

**Practical tasks**: setting up an oxy-acetylene outfit, heat-bending a flat bar to 90° and flame-straightening a bowed bar; then cutting strips from 10 mm plate (freehand and with a guide) and making a plasma cut in thin sheet.

blocks.note: The assessor watches the order you do things in: checks before lighting, the lighting order, the shut-down order. Learn the step chains in this kit until you can say them without looking.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Heating and cutting throw out heat, sparks and molten slag, use gases stored at high pressure, and make fumes. Most accidents come from **fire**, **burns**, **gas leaks** and **fumes**. Plan the job with a **risk assessment**: a written list of the hazards and how each one will be controlled.

head: Hazard
What can happen
How you control it
rows: Fire
Sparks and slag from cutting can travel 10 metres or more, fall through gaps and smoulder for a long time before flaring up.
Burnables cleared or covered
Fire watch during and after
Extinguisher at hand
Burns
Cut pieces, slag and heated bars stay hot long after they stop glowing. Hot steel looks like cold steel.
Gloves and full clothing
Tongs
Hot work marked HOT
Explosion
Containers that held fuel, oil or chemicals can explode when cut or heated. Sealed tubes and hollow parts can burst as the air inside expands.
Never cut a container until a competent person has made it safe
Vent hollow parts
Gas leaks and oxygen
Leaking fuel gas can catch fire or explode. Extra oxygen in the air makes clothing and hair burn fiercely.
Leak tests
Cylinder valves closed when not in use
Never use oxygen to blow dust or to cool yourself
Fumes
Coatings burn: zinc from galvanised steel causes metal fume fever, old paint may contain lead, and oil and plastic give off harmful smoke. Heating also makes nitrogen oxides.
Coatings removed first
Ventilation or extraction
Respirator where needed
Glare and sparks in the eyes
The flame, the hot steel and the plasma arc are bright; sparks fly at the eyes.
Goggles or face shield with the right filter shade
Falling pieces
A cut-off piece drops suddenly and can crush a foot or burn through a hose.
Plan where it will fall
Feet and hoses clear
Safety boots
Electric shock (plasma)
A plasma cutter uses a high voltage.
Dry gloves and work area
Cables checked
Isolated before parts are changed
Spalling concrete
Hot slag on a concrete floor heats the water in the concrete, which can crack and burst out in flying chips.
Cut over a cutting table with a slag tray, never straight onto concrete

head: PPE
What it protects you from
Points to check
rows: Gas welding goggles or a face shield with a filter, about shade 3 to 5 for oxy-fuel heating and cutting
Glare, heat and flying sparks
Darker for thicker cutting, as the chart says
Filter not cracked
Filter shade for plasma cutting
The plasma arc's light, which is much stronger than a flame's
Chosen from the maker's chart for the current used
Leather gauntlet gloves
Heat, hot metal, slag and sparks
Dry and without holes
Long-sleeved flame-resistant cotton or leather clothing; leather apron and sleeves for heavy cutting
Sparks and slag on the skin
Buttoned up; no turn-ups or open pockets to catch sparks
No nylon or polyester: they melt onto the skin
Free of oil and grease
Safety boots
Falling plate and hot slag
Trousers worn over the boots
Cap
Sparks in the hair
Flame-resistant material
Ear protection
Noise from plasma cutting and grinding
Worn whenever the plasma cutter or grinder is running
Respirator
Fumes from coated steel where extraction is not enough
The type the risk assessment names

head: When
What to do
rows: Before
Do the risk assessment; get a **hot work permit** for work outside the hot work bay
Move anything that can burn at least 10 m away, or cover it with fire blankets
Look behind walls, under floors, above ceilings and into gaps where sparks can fall
Never cut a drum, tank or pipe that held fuel, oil or chemicals until a competent person has cleaned it and made it safe
Have a suitable extinguisher ready; know where the alarm and the way out are
Leak-test the equipment
During
Keep hoses and cylinders away from sparks, slag and hot metal
Point the flame away from cylinders, hoses and people
Post a **fire watcher** where sparks may land out of your sight
Never leave a lit torch on the bench
After
Shut off the gas and cool or mark hot metal
Check the whole area, including below and behind the work
The fire watcher stays for a set time after the work stops, often 30 to 60 minutes, as the permit says

blocks.note: Site jobs in Jamaica often mean cutting old steel at hotels, factories and houses: wooden decks, ceiling boards, dry bush, LPG cylinders and parked vehicles may be close by. Look above, below and behind the work, cover what cannot be moved, and keep a fire watcher with an extinguisher where the sparks fall.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.note: In an emergency in Jamaica, dial 110 for fire and ambulance. For a burn, cool it under cool running water for at least 10 minutes (20 is better) and get help.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Gases, cylinders and the oxy-fuel outfit

head: Gas
What it does
Points to know
rows: Oxygen
Does not burn itself, but makes everything burn much hotter and faster. Pure oxygen burns the steel in cutting.
Stored at very high pressure
Never let oil or grease touch oxygen equipment: it can burst into flame by itself
Never use it in place of compressed air
Acetylene
Fuel gas. With oxygen it gives the hottest flame, over 3 000 °C, used for welding, heating and cutting.
Unstable at high pressure: never use it above about 100 kPa (1 bar, 15 psi)
Dissolved in acetone inside the cylinder, so the cylinder must be kept upright
Lighter than air
LPG (propane or butane)
Fuel gas, cheaper than acetylene; used for heating and cutting with the right nozzles, not for welding steel
Its flame is cooler, so preheating takes longer
Uses more oxygen
**Heavier than air**: a leak sinks into pits, drains and low corners

ul: Keep cylinders **upright and chained** to a trolley or a wall, away from heat, sparks and the slag from cutting.
Keep **acetylene** cylinders upright in use and in store, so the acetone cannot come out through the valve.
Fit the **valve cap** when a cylinder is moved or stored without its regulator. Never lift a cylinder by its valve.
Read the label: cylinder colours differ between suppliers and countries.
Open the acetylene cylinder valve **less than one and a half turns** and leave the key on it, so it can be shut at once in an emergency.

Large heating nozzles draw acetylene fast. If gas is taken out too fast, acetone comes out with it; the supplier gives a limit (often about one-seventh of the contents per hour), and big jobs may need two cylinders joined together.

head: Part
Its job
Points to know
rows: Regulator
Lowers the high cylinder pressure to a steady working pressure
**Contents gauge**: the pressure inside the cylinder
**Working gauge**: the pressure going to the torch
Adjusting screw sets the working pressure
Flashback arrestor
Fitted at each regulator outlet; stops a flame travelling back to the regulator and cylinder
Many also cut off the gas if a flashback happens
Hoses
Carry the gases to the torch
**Red** for the fuel gas; blue for oxygen (green on some American equipment)
Check valves (non-return valves)
Fitted where each hose joins the torch; let gas flow one way only
Stop the gases flowing back and mixing in the hoses
Torch shank (blowpipe)
Has the two gas valves; carries the gases to the attachment
Fits welding, heating and cutting attachments
Heating nozzle
A large nozzle with many flame holes, often called a **rosebud**, for heating a wide area
Needs high gas flows
Cutting attachment or cutting torch
Has a preheat oxygen valve and a **cutting oxygen lever**
Fitted with a cutting nozzle
Cutting nozzle
A ring of small **preheat** holes round a central hole
When the lever is pressed, **pure oxygen** comes out of the centre hole to burn and blow out the steel

blocks.note: Fuel gas nuts have **left-hand threads** and are usually notched round the outside; oxygen nuts have right-hand threads. Nozzles made for acetylene and for LPG are different: fit only the nozzle the maker lists for your fuel gas.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Choose the cutting nozzle size and the gas pressures from the **maker's chart**, by the type and thickness of the metal. A nozzle too small for the plate cuts slowly or not at all; one too big wastes gas and melts the top edge. Never copy the settings left on the outfit by the last person.

head: Mild steel thickness
Typical chart reading (acetylene cutting)
rows: A small cutting nozzle; oxygen often about 1.5–2.5 bar, acetylene about 0.15–0.3 bar
A medium nozzle; oxygen often about 2–3.5 bar, acetylene about 0.2–0.4 bar
A larger nozzle; higher oxygen pressure; acetylene still well below 1 bar

blocks.note: These figures are only a guide: nozzle systems differ widely between makers. Always use the chart for the nozzles you have, and follow the manufacturer's instructions and your instructor.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Setting up, lighting and flame control

flow: Chain both cylinders upright on the trolley
Check that the valve outlets and regulator threads are clean, undamaged and free of oil
Fit the oxygen regulator (right-hand thread) and the fuel gas regulator (left-hand thread) with the correct spanner
Fit a flashback arrestor to each regulator outlet
Check the hoses for cuts, burns and cracks; connect them the right way round, red to the fuel gas, with check valves at the torch
Fit the right nozzle for the job from the maker's chart
Wind out both regulator adjusting screws until loose; stand to one side and open the cylinder valves slowly
Set the working pressures from the chart, keeping acetylene below about 100 kPa (15 psi)
Leak-test every joint with leak-detection solution
Purge each hose in turn, in a well-ventilated place, to clear out air or mixed gas

blocks.p: Winding the adjusting screw out **before** opening the cylinder valve means no gas rushes into the regulator at full cylinder pressure, which can damage it or even set it alight. Standing to one side keeps you clear if a gauge glass bursts.

flow: Check the set-up, the pressures and the area; put on full PPE
Point the torch away from people, hoses and cylinders
Open the acetylene valve a little and light it with a **spark lighter**
Open the acetylene a little more until the flame stops giving off black smoke
Slowly open the preheat oxygen valve until each preheat flame shows a clear, sharp, rounded inner cone (neutral)
Press the cutting oxygen lever: the preheat flames may show a small feather again, so reset them to neutral with the lever held down
Check that the cutting oxygen stream is long, straight and clean; if it is ragged, shut down and clean the nozzle

head: Flame
What it looks like
Use
rows: Carburising
A white feather of extra acetylene round the inner cone
Seen while you are adjusting; not used for heating or cutting steel because it adds carbon and soot
Neutral
A clear, sharp, rounded inner cone with no feather
Heating, bending, straightening and the preheat flames for cutting
Oxidising
A short, pointed inner cone; a harsh hissing sound
Not used for heating or cutting: it burns the steel surface and wastes oxygen

head: Event
Signs
Common causes
What to do
rows: Backfire
A loud pop; the flame goes out or goes out and relights
Nozzle touching or too close to the work
Nozzle overheated or blocked with slag
Pressures too low
Loose nozzle
Close the torch valves; let the nozzle cool; clean it and check it is tight; check the pressures; relight
Flashback
The flame burns back inside the torch: a squeal or hiss, the handle gets hot, black smoke or sparks may come from the nozzle
Gases mixed in the hoses (not purged)
Wrong pressures
A blocked nozzle after a backfire
Faulty check valves
Close the torch valves at once (oxygen first, or as the maker says), then both cylinder valves. Let the torch cool. Report it; do not use the outfit again until it has been checked.

blocks.note: A torch that keeps popping is telling you something is wrong. Do not keep relighting it: find the cause first.
blocks.label: Safety

head: Job
Why heat helps
Points to know
rows: Preheating before welding
Thick steel, higher-carbon steel and cast iron cool a weld very fast, which can make it hard and cracked. Preheating slows the cooling.
Heat to the temperature the welding procedure gives, evenly over the joint area, and check it with a temperature crayon or thermometer
Freeing a seized nut or part
Heat makes the nut **expand**, loosening its grip on the bolt and breaking the rust
Heat the nut quickly so it expands before the heat soaks into the bolt
Hot bending
Red-hot steel bends with much less force and is less likely to crack
Heat evenly through the whole bend area
Flame straightening
Controlled heating and cooling shrinks the steel where you want it
See the next section
Expanding a part to fit
A heated ring, collar or pulley grows a little and can slide onto a shaft, then grips as it cools
Heat evenly; follow the drawing

blocks.p: Steel glows in different colours as it gets hotter. The colours are a guide, best seen in shade or dim light.

head: Colour of the steel
About how hot
rows: No glow (it can still burn you badly)
Below about 500 °C
Faint red, seen only in the dark
About 500–550 °C
Dull red
About 600–700 °C
Cherry red
About 750–800 °C
Bright red to orange
About 850–950 °C
Yellow
White, sparkling
1 200 °C and above: the steel is burning and being damaged

blocks.note: In bright Jamaican sunshine, red heat looks much darker or cannot be seen at all, so steel can be far hotter than it looks. Heat in the shade of the workshop, or put up a shade, and use a temperature crayon when the temperature matters.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: A **temperature crayon** (temperature-indicating crayon) is a crayon-like stick made to melt at a set temperature. Mark the work with it: when the mark melts, the steel has reached that temperature. An infrared thermometer can also be used. Both are more reliable than colour for preheating.

ul: Fit the heating nozzle the chart gives for the size of the job, and set a **neutral** flame.
Light it with a little extra acetylene first, then add oxygen; a large nozzle needs high flows, so check the cylinder can supply them.
Keep the flame **moving** over the area so it heats evenly, without hot spots or burnt patches.
Hold the tips of the inner cones a little off the surface: they must not touch the steel.

blocks.h: Heat-bending a flat bar in the vice

flow: Read the drawing and mark the bend line with soapstone
Clamp the bar in a heavy vice that is bolted down, with the bend line just above the jaws
Clear anything that can burn and have an extinguisher ready
Set a neutral flame with a heating nozzle or a large welding nozzle
Heat the whole bend area evenly, a little wider than the bar is thick, moving the flame over both faces and both edges until the steel is **bright red right through**
Pull the bar over steadily with a bending bar, or tap it over with a heavy hammer, keeping the bend at the line
Check the angle with a square while the bar is in the vice; reheat for any more bending
Let the bar cool slowly in air; handle it with tongs and mark it HOT

blocks.note: Stop bending once the colour has faded below a dull red, and reheat. Steel bent in the **blue heat** range (roughly 200–400 °C, when it shows no glow but is still very hot) can become brittle and crack.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A round bar is heated all the way round, not just on one side. If only one side is hot, the bar bends unevenly and may kink at the hot spot.

When a small area of steel is heated, it tries to **expand**. The cold metal all round it holds it in, so the hot, soft metal is squeezed and gets **thicker** instead (this is called **upsetting**). When it cools, it **shrinks**, and because it is now thicker and shorter than before, it pulls the steel around it towards the heated area. Flame straightening uses this pull to draw a bent part back into line.

blocks.note: **Heat goes on the long side.** The heated area ends up shorter, so you heat the outside (long, convex) side of a bend. Heating the inside of the bend makes the bend worse.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Pattern
How it is made
Used for
rows: V-heat (wedge heat)
A V shape marked on the face, with its wide end at the outside edge of the bend and its point about two-thirds of the way across. Heat starts at the point and works out to the wide end.
Bars, plates and sections bent edgeways (bowed along their width)
Line heat
A narrow strip heated along a line
Flanges pulled out of square by welding, and gentle bends in plate
Spot heat
Small round spots heated in a pattern
Thin sheet and plate that has buckled between welds

flow: Lay the bar on a flat bench and find the bow with a straight edge; mark the outside (long) edge at the highest point of the curve
Mark a V on the flat face: wide end at the outside edge, point about two-thirds of the way across
Set a neutral flame with a heating nozzle
Heat the V from the point outwards until it is a **dull red** right through the thickness; do not go hotter
Let the bar cool in still air
Check it with the straight edge
If it is still bowed, make another V-heat **beside** the first one, not on top of it
Handle the bar with tongs and mark it HOT

ul: Keep mild steel to a **dull red**, about 600–650 °C at most. Hotter heats damage the steel and give unpredictable results.
Several small heats are better than one large one. Check between heats.
Never heat the same spot twice: put the next heat beside the last one.
Let each heat **cool in still air**. Throwing water on it can harden and crack some steels and makes the result hard to control.
On a long bow, spread the heats along the curve, with the biggest correction at the highest point.
Use a straight edge, a string line or a square to check, never your eye alone.
Ask your instructor before straightening high-strength or treated steel: it may need a lower temperature or a different method.

blocks.note: Flame straightening is easier to do than to undo. If you put a heat in the wrong place, the bend gets worse and you must heat the other side to correct it, adding more shrinkage. Mark every heat before you light up.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Oxy-fuel cutting is a **burning** process, not a melting process. The **preheat flames** heat a small spot of steel to its **ignition (kindling) temperature**, when it glows bright red (roughly 850–900 °C, well below its melting point). Then a jet of **pure oxygen** is turned on. The hot iron burns rapidly in the oxygen and turns into liquid iron oxide, and the force of the jet blows the oxide out, leaving a narrow slot called the **kerf**. The heat of the burning helps the cut keep going as you move.
A metal can be oxy-fuel cut only if it **burns before it melts**, and if its **oxide melts at a lower temperature than the metal** so the jet can blow it away.

head: Metal
Oxy-fuel cut?
Why
rows: Mild steel and low-alloy steel
Yes, well
Iron ignites below its melting point and its oxide runs freely
Cast iron
Poorly, only with special skill
It melts at about the same temperature as it ignites
Stainless steel
No
It forms a chromium oxide skin that will not melt and flow away
Aluminium
No
It melts before it burns, and its oxide melts at a far higher temperature than the metal
Copper and brass
No
They carry heat away too fast and do not burn in the oxygen jet

blocks.p: Metals that oxy-fuel cutting cannot cut are cut with a **plasma cutter**, a saw or a grinder.

flow: Mark the line with soapstone or a scriber, and plan to cut on its **waste side**
Support the plate on the cutting table over the slag tray, with the waste free to fall clear of your feet and the hoses
Hold the nozzle square to the plate at the edge, with the tips of the preheat inner cones about **2–3 mm** above the surface
Heat the edge until it glows **bright red**
Press the cutting oxygen lever slowly and fully; as the cut breaks through, start to move
Travel at a steady speed, keeping the cones the same height and watching the sparks stream from under the plate
At the end, release the lever, lift the torch away, and let the piece fall clear

blocks.p: **Piercing** is starting a cut in the middle of a plate, away from an edge. Start in the waste, not on the line. Heat a spot to bright red, then lift the nozzle a little and tilt it, and open the cutting oxygen slowly, so the molten slag blows away from the nozzle and from you. When the jet breaks through, bring the nozzle back to its normal height and angle and move off towards the line.

ul: The **kerf** is the width of metal the cut removes, often about 1.5–3 mm with oxy-fuel. Cut on the **waste side** of the line, or the part comes out too small.
For straight cuts, run the nozzle along a **straight-edge guide**, such as a length of angle iron clamped to the plate. For circles, use a circle-cutting attachment.
Brace your arms and walk your body along the cut so the speed and height stay steady. Practise the movement with the torch unlit first.

blocks.h: What a good cut looks like

ul: A **sharp, square top edge**, not melted or rounded.
A smooth face with fine **drag lines** (the lines left on the face) that are nearly straight up and down.
A square bottom edge with only a little **slag** (dross) that knocks off easily.
The cut on the line and the part to size.

head: What you see
Likely cause
Cure
rows: Drag lines curving far back; rough face; the cut may not go through
Travel too fast, or too little cutting oxygen
Slow down; check the oxygen pressure on the chart
Melted, rounded top edge with beads of steel along it
Preheat flame too strong, nozzle too close, or travel too slow
Turn the preheat down; keep the cones 2–3 mm above; travel steadily
Heavy slag stuck to the bottom edge; wide, uneven kerf; gouges in the face
Travel too slow
Speed up to a steady pace
Wide kerf that widens down the cut; ragged face
Cutting oxygen pressure too high
Set the pressure from the chart
Slag stuck underneath; the cut slows or is lost
Cutting oxygen pressure too low, or nozzle too small
Check the chart; fit the right nozzle
Irregular cut; notches and gouges; wavering oxygen stream
Dirty or damaged nozzle
Clean it with tip cleaners, or replace it
Wavy line and uneven face
Unsteady hand or changing height
Use a guide; brace yourself; keep the height steady
Top edge bevelled and rough; slow cut
Nozzle held too high
Bring the cones back to 2–3 mm above

ul: Use **tip cleaners** of the right size: push each one straight in and out of the hole, without twisting or forcing it.
Never use a drill, a nail or wire: they enlarge or scratch the hole and spoil the flame.
Lightly dress a damaged end face flat with the file in the tip-cleaner set, as your instructor shows.
A nozzle whose holes are damaged, or that keeps backfiring after cleaning, is replaced.

blocks.p: A flame-cut edge carries slag and a skin of oxide, and on some steels a hard layer. Chip off the slag and grind the edge to **bright metal** before welding, or the weld will be porous and poorly fused.

A plasma cutter forces an electric arc through a small hole in a nozzle, with a fast stream of gas, usually **compressed air**. The squeezed arc turns the gas into **plasma**, an extremely hot, electrically charged gas. The plasma jet **melts** the metal and blows it out of the cut. Because it melts rather than burns, plasma cuts any metal that conducts electricity.

When you press the trigger, a small **pilot arc** forms inside the torch, between the electrode and the nozzle. When the torch is near the work, the arc transfers to the work through the **work clamp**, and cutting begins. The clamp must be fixed firmly to clean metal, or the cutting arc cannot form.

head: Part
Its job
rows: Power source
Supplies the DC cutting current; you set the current for the thickness
Air supply
Clean, dry compressed air at the pressure the maker gives, through a filter and regulator
Torch consumables
The **electrode**, **swirl ring**, **nozzle** (tip) and **shield cup**; they wear and are replaced
Work clamp and lead
Complete the circuit from the work back to the machine

head: Plasma cutting
Oxy-fuel cutting
rows: Cuts any metal that conducts electricity, including stainless steel and aluminium
Fast on thin metal, with a narrow kerf
Little heat, so less distortion of thin sheet
No fuel gas cylinders
Needs no electricity: works anywhere on site
Cuts thick steel well with cheaper equipment
The same outfit also heats, bends and straightens
Cuts only steel and low-alloy steel

ul: The machine uses a **high voltage**. Check the cables and torch before use, keep everything dry, and never cut standing in water.
**Switch off and isolate** the power before changing the electrode, nozzle or any torch part.
Wear a filter shade from the **maker's chart** for the current, flame-resistant clothing, gloves and **ear protection**: plasma is loud.
Cut with good ventilation or extraction: plasma makes fume and gases, especially from coated, stainless or galvanised metal.
Clear anything that can burn, as for oxy-fuel cutting.
Keep the air supply **clean and dry**: drain the water from the compressor tank and filter as the Centre's rules say. Water and oil in the air wreck the consumables and spoil the cut.

blocks.note: Jamaica's humid air puts a lot of water into a compressor's tank. If the plasma torch spits, sputters or wears out nozzles quickly, check the air for water first.
blocks.label: Jamaica

flow: Set the current and air pressure from the maker's chart for the metal and thickness
Fix the work clamp to clean metal on the job
Clamp a straight-edge guide for straight cuts
Start at the edge of the sheet, with the torch square to the surface and at the stand-off the maker gives (or with the drag shield resting on the sheet)
Press the trigger; when the arc cuts through, move steadily along the guide
Watch the sparks: they should leave straight out of the bottom of the cut
At the end, release the trigger and let the post-flow air cool the torch

head: Plasma cut fault
Likely cause
rows: Heavy dross stuck on the bottom
Travel too slow, or current too high for the thickness
Cut not through; sparks blow back up
Travel too fast, or current too low
Bevelled, uneven edge; wandering arc
Worn nozzle or electrode, or torch not held square
Arc will not start or keeps going out
Work clamp loose or on paint or rust; worn electrode; wrong air pressure

blocks.p: Check the consumables often. A nozzle whose hole has worn oval or larger, or an electrode with a deep pit in its tip, gives a poor cut and should be replaced (with the power isolated).

flow: Put the flame out at the torch, closing the torch valves in the order the maker gives
Close both cylinder valves
Open the oxygen torch valve to let the gas out of the oxygen hose and regulator, then close it; do the same for the acetylene, one gas at a time, in a ventilated place away from flames
Check that all the gauges read zero
Wind out both regulator adjusting screws until they are loose
Check that the torch valves are closed
Coil the hoses neatly and hang them off the floor, away from oil, heat and sharp edges
Leave the cylinders chained upright; fit the valve caps if the regulators are taken off

blocks.p: Releasing the adjusting screws leaves the regulators unloaded, so they are not damaged by a rush of high-pressure gas when the cylinder valves are next opened.

ul: Let the post-flow air finish cooling the torch, then switch off and isolate the machine.
Close the air supply and drain the water from the filter as the Centre's rules say.
Coil the torch lead and work lead loosely and hang them up.
Cool or mark all hot metal, and leave it where no one will pick it up by mistake.
Empty the slag tray only when it has cooled; put slag and offcuts in the right bins.
Remove sharp burrs and slag from cut pieces before they are stacked.
Put the torch, nozzles and tip cleaners away clean.
Sweep up and check the whole area for smouldering sparks before you leave.

head: What to report
Examples
What to do
rows: Equipment faults
A leaking fitting, a damaged hose, a gauge that sticks or will not return to zero, a nozzle that keeps popping, a flashback, a plasma lead with damaged insulation
Tag the item out of use, tell your instructor, and write it in the equipment log
Injuries and near misses
Burns, sparks in the eye, a small fire, a cut piece that fell near someone's feet
First aid; report and record it so the cause is fixed
Gas supply
A cylinder running low, a cylinder with no label, a damaged valve
Report it so it is changed or returned
Your job
Cuts outside the size allowed, a bar that would not straighten, faults you could not correct
Tell your instructor and record it on the job card

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise it with your instructor.

ul: I can read a drawing or job sheet and do a simple risk assessment for heating or cutting.
I can choose and check my PPE, including the right filter shade for oxy-fuel and for plasma work.
I can prevent fires before, during and after hot work, and say when a hot work permit and a fire watcher are needed.
I can explain the dangers of oxygen, acetylene and LPG, and how cylinders must be kept.
I can name the parts of an oxy-fuel outfit and say what each one does.
I can set up, leak-test and purge an oxy-acetylene outfit in the right order.
I can light a cutting torch, set a neutral preheat flame, and check the cutting oxygen.
I can recognise a backfire and a flashback and say what to do for each.
I can use heat to preheat, free a seized part and bend a bar, judging the heat by colour or with a temperature crayon.
I can explain why flame straightening works and straighten a bowed bar with V-heats.
I can explain how oxy-fuel cutting works and why it will not cut stainless steel or aluminium.
I can make a straight cut from an edge and pierce a hole, on the waste side of the line.
I can judge a cut and name cut faults with their causes and cures.
I can explain how plasma cutting works and use a plasma cutter safely.
I can shut down the outfit, clean up and report faults.

terms: Backfire
A loud pop as the flame goes into the nozzle and goes out or relights
Blue heat
Roughly 200–400 °C, when steel shows no glow; bending steel in this range can crack it
Carburising flame
A flame with extra acetylene, showing a white feather
Check valve
A one-way valve where each hose joins the torch; also called a non-return valve
Contents gauge
The regulator gauge that shows the pressure inside the cylinder
Cutting oxygen
The jet of pure oxygen from the centre hole of a cutting nozzle
Drag lines
The lines left on the face of a cut
Dross
Slag stuck to the bottom edge of a cut
Flame straightening
Using controlled heating and cooling to straighten bent steel
Flashback
A flame burning back inside the torch, with a squeal or hiss
Flashback arrestor
A safety device at each regulator outlet that stops a flame reaching the cylinder
Heating nozzle
A large nozzle with many flame holes for heating a wide area; also called a rosebud
Hot work permit
Written permission needed before heating or cutting outside the hot work bay
Ignition temperature
The temperature at which steel will burn in oxygen: bright red; also called kindling temperature
Kerf
The slot, or width of metal, removed by a cut
Neutral flame
A flame with a clear, sharp, rounded inner cone and no feather
Oxidising flame
A flame with extra oxygen: a short, pointed cone and a hiss
Piercing
Starting a cut by burning a hole through the plate away from the edge
Pilot arc
The small arc inside a plasma torch before the cutting arc transfers to the work
Plasma
A gas made so hot by an arc that it conducts electricity; used to melt and blow out metal
Preheat flames
The ring of small flames on a cutting nozzle that heat the steel to ignition temperature
Preheating
Heating steel before welding to slow the cooling of the weld
Purging
Letting each gas through its hose briefly to clear out air or mixed gas
Regulator
The device that lowers the cylinder pressure to a steady working pressure
Risk assessment
A record of a job's hazards and how each one will be controlled
Spalling
Concrete cracking and bursting when hot slag heats the water in it
Spark lighter
The flint tool used to light a gas torch
Temperature crayon
A crayon-like stick that melts at a set temperature, used to check that a part is hot enough
Tip cleaners
A set of fine wires, each sized to a nozzle hole, used to clean it
Upsetting
Hot metal being squeezed thicker when cold metal around it stops it expanding
V-heat
A wedge-shaped heat used to straighten a bar bowed edgeways
Valve cap
The cap fitted over a cylinder valve to protect it when the cylinder is moved
Working gauge
The regulator gauge that shows the pressure going to the torch

c1.title: A seized wheel nut in Ewarton
c1.text: Lascelles is asked to free a rusted wheel nut on a tipper truck at a quarry yard in Ewarton, St Catherine. The tyre is still fitted and inflated. There is a greasy rag on the hub, and the truck's diesel tank is about 2 metres from the wheel. He has an oxy-acetylene outfit with a heating nozzle.

c2.title: A bowed rail in Hayes
c2.text: At a truck-body shop in Hayes, Clarendon, Simone is flame-straightening a 75 mm × 10 mm flat bar rail that has been bowed edgeways by welding. She works on a bench by the open yard in full midday sun. Her first V-heat reduced the bow but did not remove it, and a workmate suggests throwing water on each heat to save time.

c3.title: Brackets from plate in Savanna-la-Mar
c3.text: Akeem is cutting brackets 60 mm wide from 12 mm mild steel plate with an oxy-acetylene cutting torch at a shop in Savanna-la-Mar, Westmoreland. His first brackets came out about 2 mm narrower than the drawing. One cut has heavy slag stuck along the bottom edge and a wide, uneven kerf. He notices that one preheat flame on the nozzle is short and bent to one side.

c4.title: Old balcony rails at a hotel in Negril
c4.text: A team is cutting out rusted steel balcony rails on the second floor of a hotel in Negril, Westmoreland. Below the balconies are a wooden deck, cushioned pool chairs and a walkway that guests use. The hotel's maintenance manager issues a hot work permit for the job.

c5.title: Plasma cutting for a kitchen in Falmouth
c5.text: Kimberley is plasma cutting 3 mm stainless steel sheet for a restaurant kitchen counter at a workshop in Falmouth, Trelawny. Her torch spits and sputters, and the nozzles are wearing out quickly. The shop's compressor tank has not been drained for weeks.

c6.title: Hooks for a farm gate in St Elizabeth
c6.text: Delroy is hot-bending 20 mm round bar into hooks for a farm gate at a workshop near Santa Cruz, St Elizabeth. He clamps each bar in the vice and heats it with a heating nozzle.

questions.q: Where should Lascelles direct the heat to free the nut?
o: On the stud end, until the whole stud glows bright red
Onto the nut, quickly, so it expands before the stud heats up
On the wheel rim all round the nut, so the rim expands first
On the hub behind the wheel, so that the heat travels outwards
questions.why: The nut must expand away from the stud. Heating it quickly, before the heat soaks into the stud, opens the gap and breaks the rust; heating the stud makes it expand too and grip harder.

questions.q: Why is it dangerous to heat near the wheel while the tyre is still fitted and inflated?
o: Heat can make the tyre burst, so it must come off first
The rubber melts onto the nut and makes it harder to turn
The tyre's air pressure drops and the truck may roll off the jack
The tyre gives off zinc fume that causes metal fume fever
questions.why: Heat travelling through the rim can weaken the tyre and build up pressure and gases inside it until it bursts with great force. The wheel is removed, or the tyre deflated and removed, before heat is used near it.

questions.q: What should be done about the greasy rag and the diesel tank before Lascelles lights up?
o: Nothing, as diesel does not catch fire anywhere near as easily as petrol
Soak the rag and splash the tank with water, then start heating
Keep the nozzle pointed away from the tank and work as quickly as he can
Remove the rag, shield the tank, and have an extinguisher ready
questions.why: Anything that burns is moved away or covered, and hot work near fuel needs shielding and an extinguisher at hand. Diesel and grease still burn once they are heated.

questions.q: Where should Simone put her second V-heat?
o: Exactly on top of the first one, but heated a little hotter
Beside the first one, on the outside of the bow
On the inside edge of the bow, to pull it the other way
At each end of the rail, well away from the bow
questions.why: A spot that has already been heated and upset does not respond in the same way, so each new heat goes beside the last one, on the long (outside) side of the bow.

questions.q: Her workmate says to throw water on each heat to save time. What is the best reply?
o: Yes, that is fine: the water fixes the steel in its new straight shape
Yes, but only once the heated V has turned a bright red colour
No: let it cool in still air, as quenching can harm the steel
No: water cools it too slowly to make any real difference
questions.why: Each heat is left to cool in still air. Quenching can harden and crack some steels and makes the amount of straightening hard to control.

questions.q: Why is it hard for Simone to judge a dull red heat on this job?
o: Bright sun hides the glow, so the steel may be hotter than it looks
The flat bar is far too thick for any red colour to show on its surface
Steel heated out in the open air never shows any red colour at all
The bright neutral flame hides the colour of the steel underneath it
questions.why: In bright sun, red heat looks darker or cannot be seen, so it is easy to overheat. Work in shade and use a temperature crayon when the temperature matters.

questions.q: What is the most likely reason Akeem's brackets came out 2 mm too narrow?
o: The steel plate shrank by 2 mm as it cooled after each cut
The preheat flames were set a little carburising for the job
He cut down the middle of the line, not its waste side
He used a cutting nozzle one size too small for the plate
questions.why: The cut removes a slot (the kerf) about 1.5–3 mm wide. If the nozzle follows the line itself, half the kerf comes out of the part, so cuts are made on the waste side of the line.

questions.q: What most likely caused the heavy slag stuck along the bottom and the wide, uneven kerf?
o: Travelling too slowly
Travelling much too fast
Cones held 2–3 mm above the plate
Preheat cones too far from the plate
questions.why: When the torch moves too slowly, the cut widens and gouges, and slag builds up and sticks along the bottom edge. Travelling too fast gives drag lines that curve back and may lose the cut.

questions.q: What should Akeem do about the short, bent preheat flame?
o: Turn the preheat oxygen up until all the flames look even
Carry on: the other preheat flames will make up for it
Open the hole out with a small drill bit to clear it
Shut down and clean the hole with the right tip cleaner
questions.why: A short, crooked flame means a hole partly blocked with slag. A tip cleaner of the right size, pushed straight in and out, clears it without damaging the hole; a drill would enlarge it.

questions.q: Before welding the brackets to a frame, how should Akeem prepare the flame-cut edges?
o: Wire-brush off only the loose slag and weld straight over the oxide
Chip off the slag and grind the edges to bright metal
Paint the edges with primer so that they do not rust first
Heat the edges to red again to burn off the oxide skin
questions.why: The oxide skin and slag on a cut edge cause porosity and poor fusion. Grinding back to bright metal gives a clean edge for welding.

questions.q: Sparks from the cutting will fall onto the deck and the pool chairs below. What does the job need?
o: The area below cleared or covered, with a fire watcher
Only a warning sign at the top of the stairs to the balconies
Cutting faster, so that fewer sparks have time to fall
A bucket of water on the balcony beside the person cutting
questions.why: Sparks can travel 10 m or more and smoulder unseen. The chairs are moved, the deck is covered with fire blankets, and a watcher with an extinguisher covers the area where the sparks land.

questions.q: How should the guests on the walkway be protected?
o: Ask them to wear sunglasses whenever they walk past below
Close the walkway with barriers and signs during the work
Let them hurry past whenever the cutting torch is not lit
Cut only early in the morning, before most guests are up
questions.why: Falling slag, cut pieces and sparks can injure people below. The area is closed off with barriers and signs, and the permit's conditions are followed; sunglasses give no protection from slag.

questions.q: The permit says the fire watch continues after the work stops. Why?
o: The cut rails need time to finish changing shape as they cool
The gas left in the hoses may leak once they cool off
The hotel needs time to check the new rails for size
A hidden spark can smoulder in the deck and flare up later
questions.why: Sparks lodged in timber, cushions or gaps can smoulder for a long time before flames appear. The watcher stays for the time the permit sets, often 30 to 60 minutes.

questions.q: What is the most likely cause of the spitting torch and fast-wearing nozzles?
o: The stainless sheet is too thin for a plasma cutter
Water in the compressed air from the undrained tank
The work clamp is fixed too close to the cut
The air pressure is set exactly as the chart says
questions.why: Moisture and oil in the air make the arc sputter and rapidly wear the electrode and nozzle. The compressor tank and filter must be drained regularly, especially in humid weather.

questions.q: Which sign tells Kimberley that a plasma nozzle needs replacing?
o: Its outside has turned a light straw colour
It feels warm after a long cut
Its hole has worn oval or larger
It makes a hissing sound during post-flow
questions.why: A worn, oval or enlarged nozzle hole lets the arc wander, giving bevelled edges and heavy dross. Replace it with the power isolated; some colour and warmth are normal.

questions.q: Compared with small oxy-fuel cuts, which extra PPE does plasma cutting need?
o: Only clear safety glasses, because plasma makes no flame at all
Rubber gloves in place of leather, because plasma uses electricity
A darker filter shade from the maker's chart, and ear protection
Nothing extra: the same gas goggles and gloves are good enough
questions.why: The plasma arc gives off far more light and UV than a cutting flame, so the shade comes from the maker's chart for the current, and the process is loud. Leather gloves are still worn: rubber gloves melt.

questions.q: How should Delroy heat each bar before bending it?
o: Evenly all the way round, over the whole length of the bend
On the inside of the bend only, until it starts to melt
On one side only, so that the bar bends towards the cold side
Along the whole bar from end to end, so it stays straight
questions.why: A round bar heated on one side bends unevenly and can kink. Heating evenly all round and along the bend area to bright red lets it bend smoothly at the line.

questions.q: Delroy keeps bending a hook after the glow has gone. Why is this a problem?
o: Cooled steel cannot be heated again for bending later
Steel bent at the blue heat can turn brittle and crack
The bend will spring back to a straight bar overnight
Steel bent cold always becomes too soft to hold its shape
questions.why: Steel worked in the blue heat range (roughly 200–400 °C) can become brittle and crack. Stop when the colour fades below dull red, and reheat.

questions.q: Marlon's cutting torch keeps popping and going out while he cuts close to the plate. What is the most likely cause?
o: The cutting oxygen pressure is too high
The preheat flame is set exactly neutral
The plate has a light coat of mill scale
The nozzle is too close and overheating
questions.why: Repeated backfires come from a nozzle touching or too close to the work, an overheated or blocked nozzle, or low pressures. Close the valves, let it cool, clean it and hold it 2–3 mm above the plate.

questions.q: When piercing a hole in 15 mm plate, why do you lift and tilt the nozzle as you open the cutting oxygen?
o: So the slag blows away from the nozzle and from you
So the preheat flames can reach the far side of the plate
So the cutting oxygen uses less pressure as it breaks through
So the kerf comes out narrower than at an edge start
questions.why: At first the molten slag has nowhere to go but up. Lifting and tilting the nozzle sends it away, so it does not block the nozzle, cause a backfire or hit you.
